hero.title: About Global Governance Frameworks
hero.subtitle: An open-source effort to help humanity thrive within a regenerating biosphere—through governance that coordinates planetary responsibility while protecting local autonomy and diversity.

purpose.title: The Purpose
purpose.opening: Global Governance Frameworks began with a simple question: What would it take for the planet and humanity to thrive?
purpose.statement: The purpose of Global Governance Frameworks is to expand humanity’s capacity to thrive within a regenerating biosphere, while protecting dignity, distributed agency, cultural plurality, and the freedom of future generations.
purpose.closing: This is not a single global target to be maximized. It is a constitutional direction: a test for whether institutions, economies, and technologies are increasing the conditions for life to flourish—or consuming the foundations on which flourishing depends.

diagnosis.title: Why New Governance Architecture Is Needed
diagnosis.paragraph1: Many of today’s institutions were built to preserve states, organizations, markets, and economic flows. They can produce extraordinary benefits, but planetary wellbeing is often treated as a secondary concern, an externality, or the responsibility of no actor with sufficient authority.
diagnosis.paragraph2: Climate disruption, financial contagion, pandemics, technological risks, migration, and ecosystem decline cross national and institutional boundaries. The systems producing these problems are globally coupled, while the institutions responsible for addressing them remain fragmented by jurisdiction, mandate, and timescale.
diagnosis.callout: The challenge is not simply to make existing institutions work harder. It is to make human and planetary thriving causally effective in the architecture of governance itself.

whatItIs.title: What GGF Is—and Is Not
whatItIs.intro: Global Governance Frameworks is a growing ecosystem of practical governance blueprints, protocols, and implementation tools. It is designed to connect action across scales without imposing one model everywhere.

items.title: Not a world government
items.description: GGF proposes coordination where problems are genuinely shared, while keeping decisions at the lowest level capable of handling them.

items.title: Not a finished doctrine
items.description: The frameworks are open to testing, criticism, adaptation, replacement, and local reinterpretation.

items.title: Not only a vision
items.description: The work specifies institutions, rights, funding mechanisms, accountability structures, transition pathways, and implementation tools.

items.title: Not one-size-fits-all
items.description: The architecture is modular and interoperable so communities can retain sovereignty, culture, and contextual intelligence.

transition.title: How Change Begins
transition.intro: GGF does not assume that humanity must first secure universal agreement or comprehensively reform the United Nations. Change can begin wherever willing actors have enough trust, authority, and capacity to act.

steps.title: Begin with willing actors
steps.description: Communities, cities, Indigenous nations, civil-society networks, public institutions, businesses, and states can adopt useful parts without waiting for everyone else.

steps.title: Build in protected real-world spaces
steps.description: Pilot new arrangements at a scale where failure is survivable, learning is rapid, and affected communities retain meaningful control.

steps.title: Evaluate openly and adapt
steps.description: Measure human, ecological, and institutional outcomes; publish failures as well as successes; and revise the frameworks in response to evidence.

steps.title: Connect what works
steps.description: Use shared protocols and standards to let successful initiatives exchange resources, knowledge, legitimacy, and support without erasing their differences.

steps.title: Let demonstrated value attract adoption
steps.description: Expansion should come because participation improves resilience, agency, wellbeing, and regenerative capacity—not because conformity is imposed.

steps.title: Transform the wider system
steps.description: As the coalition becomes more capable, it can interoperate with, reform, or eventually replace structures that no longer serve their stated purpose.

transition.principle: The strategy is to bypass unanimity and veto bottlenecks at the point of initiation—not to bypass affected communities, democratic consent, or accountability.

accountability.title: Holding the Project to Its Purpose
accountability.intro: A system’s real purpose is revealed not by its language, but by what its feedbacks reward and what it sacrifices when goals conflict. GGF should therefore be judged by its behavior, not only by its aspirations.

tests.title: Regeneration before expansion
tests.description: More adopters are not success if ecological integrity, dignity, or local agency deteriorate.

tests.title: Outcomes before activity
tests.description: Documents, meetings, funding, and institutional growth matter only when they improve conditions in the world.

tests.title: Agency before administrative convenience
tests.description: Coordination must not become an excuse to centralize decisions that communities can govern themselves.

tests.title: Truth before coalition unity
tests.description: Bad news, dissent, and failed experiments must remain visible even when they complicate expansion.

tests.title: Purpose before institutional survival
tests.description: Any GGF body should be changed, transferred, or ended when preserving it no longer serves the mission it was created to advance.

accountability.closing: A framework that grows while degrading the foundations of thriving is not succeeding. This commitment is why transparent evaluation, plural oversight, and the ability to revise or sunset institutions belong inside the architecture.

list.name: Subsidiarity
list.description: Decisions belong at the lowest effective level, with higher levels supporting rather than absorbing local capacity.

list.name: Interoperability
list.description: Different governance systems should be able to coordinate without becoming identical.

list.name: Regeneration
list.description: Institutions should restore the ecological and social substrates on which their own success depends.

list.name: Sovereignty and plurality
list.description: Coordination must protect cultural difference, Indigenous sovereignty, and multiple legitimate ways of organizing collective life.

list.name: Transparency and contestability
list.description: Claims, decisions, metrics, and power structures must remain open to challenge by genuinely independent observers.

list.name: Evolutionary design
list.description: Frameworks should learn, adapt, and retire components that no longer fit changing realities.

currentReality.title: The Current Reality: An Open Project Seeking Co-Builders
currentReality.paragraph1: Global Governance Frameworks is not yet a formal organization. It is currently an independent project initiated by Björn Kenneth Holmström, developed openly and offered to those who may be able to test, challenge, improve, or implement it.
currentReality.paragraph2: The ecosystem is substantial but uneven in maturity. Some frameworks are detailed design documents; others remain exploratory. None should be treated as validated at planetary scale merely because it is comprehensive on paper.
currentReality.paragraph3: That is not a disclaimer at the edge of the project—it is part of its design. GGF can become a credible governance ecosystem only through collaboration with affected communities, practitioners, researchers, public institutions, and funders willing to subject the work to reality.

origins.title: How This Work Began
origins.paragraph1: The project grew from a long-running inquiry into a foundational question: What would it take for humanity and the living planet to thrive together? It began with the book Global Governance: Natural Steps Toward a Thriving World and expanded into a connected ecosystem of frameworks for implementation.
origins.paragraph2: The scope widened because the problems are coupled. Peace cannot be separated from economic security; ecological regeneration cannot be separated from law and finance; global coordination cannot endure without local legitimacy, cultural integrity, and meaningful agency.

development.title: How the Frameworks Are Developed
development.paragraph1: The work combines systems thinking, institutional design, comparative research, iterative critique, and open-source development. Frameworks are treated as hypotheses about governance: they should become more precise through challenge and more modest where evidence does not support them.
development.paragraph2: Advanced AI systems—including Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, Grok, and DeepSeek—have served as research, critique, simulation, and drafting partners. Their contribution increases analytical breadth, but agreement among AI systems is not validation, and responsibility for the published work remains human.
development.paragraph3: The decisive forms of validation must come from domain expertise, Indigenous and community authority, empirical evaluation, and real implementation under conditions where consequences matter.

moreResources.title: Explore the Research and Resources
moreResources.description: Browse books, whitepapers, articles, tools, and supporting research on governance, systems thinking, and implementation.

seekingCollaborators.title: Building the “We” Together
seekingCollaborators.paragraph1: Throughout the frameworks, “we” names the collective capacity the project is trying to help create—not an established institution speaking on behalf of humanity.
seekingCollaborators.paragraph2: The project becomes genuinely plural only when people with different forms of knowledge and lived experience can shape its priorities, challenge its assumptions, and own the implementations that affect them.
seekingCollaborators.paragraph3: The frameworks are released under open licenses. Communities and organizations may use and adapt them without permission, provided implementation respects the rights, sovereignty, and integrity of those involved.

foundersNote.title: A Note from the Initiator
foundersNote.paragraph1: These frameworks are not abstract theories for me. They grew from a lifelong inquiry into humanity’s potential, experiences of profound interconnectedness, and an equally direct encounter with suffering—both in the world and in my own life.
foundersNote.paragraph2: I have tried to hold the vision and the reality together: neither reducing governance to technical machinery nor allowing compassion and aspiration to remain without practical structure.
foundersNote.paragraph3: What is offered here is not a final answer or a claim to speak for others. It is scaffolding: an invitation to test whether we can build forms of coordination worthy of the living world they are meant to serve.

whatWeNeed.title: What This Project Needs
whatWeNeed.paragraph1: Moving from blueprints to functioning institutions requires people who can test the work from perspectives the current project cannot supply on its own:

needs.description: Places willing to adapt and test selected frameworks under real conditions.

needs.category: Indigenous governance authorities and knowledge holders
needs.description: Partnership grounded in sovereignty, consent, reciprocity, and protection against extraction or appropriation.
Experience translating institutional ideas into law, administration, facilitation, and durable practice.
Independent scrutiny, empirical testing, and methods that serve participating communities.
Open, community-controlled infrastructure for coordination, transparency, and data sovereignty.
Patient support for pilots, evaluation, organizational development, and public-interest infrastructure.
Help making the work accessible, culturally legible, and open to publics beyond policy and research circles.

whatWeNeed.paragraph2: Participation should not mean endorsing the whole ecosystem. A valuable contribution may be to implement one useful component, identify a serious flaw, or show that a proposed mechanism should not be used.

contribute.title: Challenge or Contribute
contribute.description: Share criticism, domain knowledge, proposals, or evidence that can make the frameworks more grounded.

join.title: Help Build the Commons
join.description: Connect with the project, contribute to its open-source infrastructure, or help develop a collaborative network.

apply.title: Test a Framework
apply.description: Adapt a useful component in your community or organization, with transparent learning and no requirement to adopt the whole system.
